tool.name: Markdown
tool.tagline: Plain-text formatting for READMEs, docs, notes and comments
tool.description: Markdown turns plain text with a few punctuation conventions into formatted HTML. It is the format of READMEs, GitHub issues and pull requests, documentation sites, chat apps and note-taking tools, and CommonMark plus GitHub Flavored Markdown define exactly how it is parsed.

glossary.def: The precise, agreed specification of Markdown that most modern Markdown tools follow, so the same text is formatted the same way everywhere.
GitHub's version of Markdown: CommonMark plus extras such as tables, task lists and strikethrough. Many other sites support it too.
A short written description of an image, shown if the image can't load and read aloud by screen readers for people who can't see it.
A bit of code inside a sentence, written between backticks like `this`, shown in a typewriter-style font with no formatting applied.
Several lines of code between two lines of three backticks (or tildes), shown exactly as written; a language name after the opening backticks turns on colouring.
The word right after the opening backticks of a fenced code block, usually a language name like python, which display tools use to colour the code.
Showing code with different colours for different kinds of words and symbols, to make it easier to read.
Quoted text set apart from the rest, written by starting lines with >.
A horizontal line across the page separating sections, written as --- (or *** or ___) on a line of its own.
A Markdown rule that lets a line continuing a paragraph inside a quote or list item leave out the > or indentation the other lines need.
A list whose items start with [ ] or [x], shown as empty or ticked checkboxes.
A note marked in the text with [^1] and written out separately; it is shown at the bottom of the page with a link back.
A quote block starting with [!NOTE], [!TIP], [!IMPORTANT], [!WARNING] or [!CAUTION], which GitHub shows as a coloured box.
A link written as [text][label] with the address given once elsewhere, on a line like [label]: https://example.com.
The name a display tool gives each heading, such as #getting-started, so links can jump straight to that section.
A chunk of raw HTML in a Markdown file starting with a tag like <div>; it lasts until the next blank line, and Markdown inside it isn't formatted.
A block of settings (title, date, tags) written in YAML between two --- lines at the very top of a Markdown file, read by website-building tools.
Markdown that can also contain interactive web page components, used by some documentation sites. It is stricter than plain Markdown.
In CommonMark, a block that can hold other blocks: a quote, a list or a list item.
In CommonMark, a block that holds only text, never other blocks: a paragraph, heading, code block, HTML block or horizontal line.
A list with no blank lines between its items (tight) is shown compactly; one blank line anywhere makes it loose, with paragraph spacing for every item.
A row of * or _ characters. CommonMark checks the characters on each side of a run (whether it is left- or right-flanking) to decide if it can start or end emphasis.

concepts.name: Paragraphs, line breaks and emphasis
concepts.summary: Separate paragraphs with blank lines, force a line break with a backslash at the end of a line, and mark *italic*, **bold** and `code`.
concepts.why: These few rules cover most of what people type in project notes, comments and chat apps.
concepts.body:
**Markdown** is a simple way to format text using ordinary characters you can type on any keyboard. You write `**bold**`, and wherever the text is displayed it shows up in bold. The file itself stays **plain text**: just characters, with no hidden formatting the way a Word document has, so it's easy to read even before it's formatted.

Programs that display Markdown **render** it: they turn the marks into formatted text, usually by converting it to **HTML**, the language web pages are written in. Markdown is used for **README** files (the introduction page of a software project), documentation, notes apps, chat apps, and comments on GitHub, a website where people share projects.

**Paragraphs** are groups of lines separated by one or more **blank lines**. A single line break inside a paragraph does *not* start a new line in the result: the lines are joined into one, so you can wrap long text in your editor however you like.

To force a line break inside a paragraph, end the line with a backslash `\` or with two or more spaces. The backslash is better, because spaces at the end of a line are invisible and editors often delete them. (Some places, like GitHub comments and many chat apps, treat every line break as a real one; Markdown files usually don't.)

Formatting inside a line:

- `*italic*` or `_italic_` for *italic*;
- `**bold**` or `__bold__` for **bold**, and `***both***`;
- backticks around text for `code`: shown in a typewriter-style font, with no formatting applied inside. Writers use it for commands, file names and small pieces of program code.

Prefer `*` inside words: `un*frigging*believable` works, while underscores inside a word are ignored, so a name like `snake_case_name` stays intact.

To show a character that would otherwise format text, put a backslash in front of it: `\*not italic\*`. This works for any punctuation character.
concepts.code: This is the first paragraph. These two lines are joined into one line in the output. This is a second paragraph, after a blank line.\ This line starts after a forced line break (trailing backslash). Some *italic*, some **bold**, some ***bold italic***, and some `inline_code()`. snake_case_stays_as_is, but un*believ*able works. \*literal asterisks\*
takeaways: Blank lines separate paragraphs; single line breaks are joined
End a line with \ (or two spaces) to force a line break
*italic*, **bold**, `code`; put a backslash before a mark to show it as is
pitfalls: Expecting a single line break to start a new line in a formatted README.

quiz.q: Two lines of text are separated by a single line break and no blank line. How does standard Markdown display them?
options: As one paragraph with the lines joined
With a forced line break between them
quiz.explain: A single line break inside a paragraph is shown as a space, so the lines run together.

concepts.name: Headings and lists
concepts.summary: Structure documents with # headings, and write bullet lists with - and numbered lists with 1., nesting them by indentation.
concepts.why: Headings and lists give a document its skeleton and make it easy to skim.
concepts.body:
**Headings** start with one to six `#` characters followed by a space: `# Title`, `## Section`, `### Subsection`. More `#` means a smaller, lower-level heading. Use a single `#` heading per document for the title, and don't skip levels (no `###` straight after `#`): many tools build a table of contents, and links to each section, from your headings. (You may also see an older style that underlines a heading with `===` or `---`; you needn't write it.)

**Bullet lists** use `-`, `*` or `+` followed by a space. Pick one and stick to it; switching to a different one starts a new list.

**Numbered lists** use a number followed by `.` or `)`. Only the **first** number matters: it sets where counting starts, and the rest are numbered in order automatically. So writing `1.` on every line is a common habit: when you reorder items, no numbers need changing.

**Nesting**: to put a list inside a list item, indent it so its marker lines up with the **text** of the item above. That's two spaces under `- ` and three under `1. `. Extra paragraphs inside an item use the same indentation.

Leave a blank line before a list that follows a paragraph. Some tools need it, and without it a numbered list that doesn't start at 1 stays part of the paragraph.
concepts.code:
# Pancakes

## Steps

1. Mix the batter:
   - 200 g flour
   - 2 eggs and 300 ml milk
1. Rest it for 10 minutes
1. Fry in a hot pan

## Notes

- Serves four
- Keeps for two days
  - in the fridge
  - or frozen

<!-- the numbered list shows as 1. 2. 3. even though every item says 1. -->
takeaways: # to ###### followed by a space make headings; one # title per document
- for bullets, 1. for numbered lists; only the first number matters
Indent sub-lists to line up with the parent item's text
pitfalls: Writing #Heading without a space, which is shown as a plain paragraph instead of a heading.

quiz.q: An ordered list is written 3. / 1. / 7. on three lines. How is it numbered?
quiz.explain: The first number sets the start and the following items count up from it.

concepts.name: Links and images
concepts.summary: Write links [text](url "title"), images ![alt](src), automatic links in angle brackets, and links to other files and to sections.
concepts.why: Documents link to each other constantly, and good image descriptions make pages usable by everyone.
concepts.body: A link is written `[link text](url)`: the words people click go in square brackets, and the web address, the **URL**, goes in round brackets right after. You can add a title that appears when the mouse hovers over the link: `[docs](https://example.com "Read the docs")`. The address can also point to another file of the same project, written as the way to get there from the current file's folder: `[setup guide](docs/setup.md)` links to `setup.md` inside the `docs` folder. An **image** is the same with a `!` in front: `![alt text](images/diagram.png)`. The **alt text** is a short description that is shown when the image can't load, and read aloud by screen readers (programs that read the screen out for blind and partially sighted people). So describe what the image shows, rather than writing "image". Markdown can't set an image's size. When you need that, write the image as HTML instead: ``. **Automatic links**: put a web address or an email address between angle brackets, ``, and it becomes clickable. On GitHub, plain `https://` and `www.` addresses become links even without the brackets. To link to a section of the same page, use `#` plus the heading's text in lower case, with spaces turned into hyphens and most punctuation left out. On GitHub, `## Getting started` is reached with `[see below](#getting-started)`. Put an image inside a link's square brackets to make the image clickable: `[![build status](badge.svg)](https://ci.example.com)`. Many project pages show small status pictures, called badges, this way. Addresses containing spaces or brackets need care: replace each space with `%20`, or wrap the whole address in angle brackets: `[file]()`.
concepts.code: See the [installation guide](docs/install.md) or the [website](https://example.com "Project homepage"). Jump to [Getting started](#getting-started). ![Map: the cafe is two streets north of the station](docs/map.png) [![Build status](https://ci.example.com/badge.svg)](https://ci.example.com/project) Contact: or ## Getting started
takeaways: [text](url "title") for links, ![alt](src) for images
A path like docs/setup.md links another file; #section-name links a heading
Write meaningful alt text; use HTML when size matters
pitfalls: Putting a space between ] and ( as in [text] (url), which breaks the link.

quiz.q: How do you make the image badge.svg clickable, so it opens a status page?
quiz.explain: The whole image goes inside the square brackets of an ordinary link.

concepts.name: Code spans and code blocks
concepts.summary: Show code inside a sentence with backticks and in fenced blocks with ```, naming the language for colouring; know the indented form and how to show backticks.
concepts.why: Code is the most common content in technical writing, and fences with language tags make it readable.
concepts.body:
**Code spans** wrap a bit of code inside a sentence in backticks: `` `git status` ``. Inside, no formatting happens, so `*` and `_` show as typed. To include a backtick, surround the span with two backticks instead of one, with a space inside each end: ``` `` a`b `` ```.

**Fenced code blocks** use three (or more) backticks or tildes on their own lines:

````
```python
def greet(name):
    return f"hello {name}"
```
````

- The word after the opening fence is the **info string**, normally the name of the programming language the code is written in (`python`, `bash`, `json`, `diff`). Display tools use it for **syntax highlighting**: colouring different kinds of words. GitHub also turns `mermaid` blocks into diagrams.
- The closing fence must use the same character and be at least as long. To show a fence inside a block, wrap it in a longer fence (four backticks), as above.
- Everything inside shows exactly as typed: no backslashes needed.

**Indented code blocks**: lines indented by four spaces also form a code block. They can't carry a language and are easy to create by accident (for example, an over-indented paragraph after a list), so prefer fences.

Use `diff` blocks to show changes (lines starting with `+` and `-` get coloured as added and removed), `console` or `shell` for commands typed into a terminal, and keep lines short, since code blocks scroll sideways instead of wrapping.
concepts.code:
Run `npm install` and then `` npm run `build` `` (a span containing backticks).

```bash
npm install
npm run build
```

```diff
- const port = 3000;
+ const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
```

~~~markdown
```js
console.log("a fence shown inside a block");
```
~~~

    indented by four spaces: also a code block, but no language
takeaways: Backticks for inline code; ``` fences with a language for blocks
Use a longer fence to show a fence inside a block
Prefer fences over four-space indented blocks
pitfalls: Indenting a paragraph four spaces by accident and having it render as a code block.

quiz.q: You need to show a fenced code block, including its ``` lines, inside your document. What works?
options: Wrap it in a fence of four backticks (or tildes)
quiz.explain: The outer fence must be longer than or different from any fence inside it, so ```` or ~~~ contains ``` lines.

concepts.name: Blockquotes, rules and escaping
concepts.summary: Quote text with >, separate sections with ---, and use backslashes to show characters that would otherwise be read as Markdown.
concepts.why: Quotes appear constantly in issues and reviews, and backslashes are how you write text that looks like formatting marks.
concepts.body:
A **blockquote** prefixes lines with `>`. It can contain any Markdown: paragraphs, lists, code, even nested quotes with `> >`. A blank line ends it; a blank line that starts with `>` keeps it going with a new paragraph inside.

Thanks to a rule called **lazy continuation**, a line that continues a paragraph inside a quote doesn't need its own `>`, but adding it to every line is clearer.

A **thematic break** (a horizontal line across the page) is a line of three or more `-`, `*` or `_`, optionally with spaces: `---`. Watch out: `---` directly under a line of text turns that text into a **heading** (an older heading style). Leave a blank line before it, or use `***`.

**Escaping**: a backslash before any punctuation character makes it show as is: `\#`, `\*`, `\_`, `\[`, `\>`, `\-`, `\\`. Common needs:

- a line starting with a number and period that isn't a list: `2026\. A good year`;
- a leading `#` or `>` that isn't a heading or quote;
- literal asterisks or underscores around words.

Inside code spans and code blocks, backslashes are literal and nothing needs escaping. HTML's named characters, such as `©` for ©, also work, but typing the character itself is usually simpler.
concepts.code:
> **Note**
> Quoted text can contain *formatting*,
>
> multiple paragraphs,
> - and lists.
>
> > A nested quote.

Paragraph text.

---

2026\. A great year (not a list item).
\# Not a heading
Use \*asterisks\* literally, and `*here*` no escaping is needed.

Heading by accident
---
takeaways: > quotes any Markdown, including nested quotes
--- after a blank line is a rule; directly under text it makes a heading
Put a backslash before punctuation to show it as is
pitfalls: Putting --- directly under a paragraph to draw a line and getting a heading instead.

quiz.q: How do you write a paragraph that begins with 1984. without it becoming a list?
quiz.explain: The backslash before the period stops the line from looking like the start of a numbered list.

concepts.name: Tables (GFM)
concepts.summary: Build tables from | characters and a row of dashes, line columns up left, centre or right with colons, and know their limits.
concepts.why: Tables are the clearest way to show options, settings and comparisons in docs.
concepts.body:
**Tables** come from **GitHub Flavored Markdown** (GFM), GitHub's extended version of Markdown. They work almost everywhere (GitHub, GitLab, most documentation sites, editors' previews), but they aren't part of **CommonMark**, the core Markdown standard. ```markdown | Option | Default | Description | | -------- | :-----: | ------------------ | | `port` | 8080 | Port to listen on | ``` - The first row is the header; the second is the **separator row** of dashes, which is required. - Colons set alignment: `:---` left, `:---:` centre, `---:` right. - The `|` at the start and end of each row is optional, and the columns don't have to line up in the source, though aligned source is easier to read. - Cells contain inline Markdown only: code, emphasis, links. No block content such as lists or multiple paragraphs; use `
` for a line break if the renderer allows HTML. - Write a `|` character inside a cell as `\|`, even inside code spans in a table. - The table ends at a blank line or at a line that clearly starts something else, such as a heading. For anything complex (merged cells, multi-paragraph cells) use an HTML table, a list of sections, or a definition-style layout instead. Tools that tidy Markdown files, such as Prettier, line the columns up for you, which keeps the source readable.
concepts.code:
| Command       | Alias | Time (s) | Notes                     |
| :------------ | :---: | -------: | ------------------------- |
| `make build`  | `mb`  |     12.5 | Compiles everything       |
| `make test`   | `mt`  |      4.0 | Runs **unit** tests       |
| `grep a\|b`   |       |      0.1 | Pipe escaped inside a cell |

Rows don't need aligned pipes:

Name | Value
--- | ---
x | 1
takeaways: Header row, then a --- separator row, then data rows
Colons in the separator row set left, centre or right alignment
Cells hold inline content only; escape | as \|
pitfalls: Trying to put a bullet list inside a table cell; it renders as literal text.

quiz.q: What does the separator cell ---: do?
quiz.explain: A colon on the right side of the dashes right-aligns that column; colons on both sides centre it.

concepts.name: Task lists, strikethrough, footnotes, alerts
concepts.summary: Use GitHub's extras: - [ ] task lists, ~~strikethrough~~, bare-URL autolinks, footnotes, alerts like > [!NOTE], and @mentions and #123 links.
concepts.why: These features turn Markdown into a collaboration tool in issues, pull requests and READMEs.
concepts.body:
GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM) adds features beyond CommonMark, and GitHub adds a few more on top:

- **Task lists**: `- [ ] todo` and `- [x] done` render checkboxes; in GitHub issues (task and problem reports) and pull requests (proposed changes) they're clickable and show progress.
- **Strikethrough**: `~~removed~~`.
- **Extended autolinks**: bare `https://...` and `www.` URLs become links without angle brackets.
- **Footnotes**: `Text[^1]` with `[^1]: The note.` anywhere in the document; rendered at the bottom with back-links.
- **Alerts**: a blockquote starting with `[!NOTE]`, `[!TIP]`, `[!IMPORTANT]`, `[!WARNING]` or `[!CAUTION]` renders as a coloured callout.
- **References** in issues, pull requests and comments: `@user` mentions, `#123` issue links, commit IDs and `owner/repo#123` become links.
- **Emoji shortcodes** like `:rocket:`.

GFM also blocks some HTML tags that could be abused (such as `<script>` and `<iframe>`).

Portability varies. Task lists, tables and strikethrough are widely supported; footnotes and alerts less so; mentions and issue references only mean something on GitHub (GitLab has similar but not identical syntax). If a document is rendered in several places, such as GitHub and a docs site, check the features against both.
concepts.code:
## Release checklist

- [x] Update the changelog
- [ ] Tag the release
- [ ] ~~Announce on the mailing list~~ (moved to the blog)

> [!WARNING]
> Version 3 removes the legacy API.

Fixes #142, thanks @ana-dev. See https://example.com/notes for details.

The parser is linear-time[^re2].

[^re2]: It uses an automaton-based engine, so no input can cause backtracking.
takeaways: - [ ] and - [x] make task lists; ~~text~~ strikes through
> [!NOTE] style blockquotes render as alerts on GitHub
Footnotes, mentions and #refs aren't supported by every renderer
pitfalls: Using GitHub-only features like alerts or #123 references in docs that are also rendered elsewhere.

quiz.q: Which syntax creates a GitHub alert box?
options: > [!NOTE] on the first line of a blockquote
quiz.explain: GitHub recognises a blockquote whose first line is [!NOTE] (or TIP, IMPORTANT, WARNING, CAUTION).

concepts.name: Reference links and heading anchors
concepts.summary: Keep paragraphs readable with reference-style links [text][id] and definitions at the bottom, and link reliably to headings.
concepts.why: Long docs with many links stay editable when URLs live in one place instead of inside every sentence.
concepts.body: **Reference-style links** separate the link from its URL: ```markdown Read the [style guide][guide] and the [API docs][]. [guide]: https://example.com/style "Style guide" [API docs]: https://example.com/api ``` - `[text][label]` uses the definition with that label; labels are case-insensitive. - `[text][]` (collapsed) and `[text]` (shortcut) use the text itself as the label. - Definitions `[label]: url "optional title"` can appear anywhere and render as nothing; put them at the end of a section or file. - The same works for images: `![logo][logo-img]`. Benefits: paragraphs read like prose, a URL used five times is defined once, and changing it is one edit. If a label has no definition, the brackets are left as literal text, which makes typos easy to spot. **Heading anchors**, the names that let a link jump to a heading, aren't standard Markdown; each display tool makes up its own. GitHub lower-cases the text, removes punctuation except hyphens and underscores, replaces spaces with hyphens and appends `-1`, `-2` for duplicates. Other tools (MkDocs, Docusaurus, Hugo) use similar but not identical rules, and some support explicit IDs such as `## Install {#install}`. For links that must stay stable across renderers and heading edits, add an explicit anchor with HTML: ``.
concepts.code:
Our [contributing guide][contrib] explains the workflow. Questions go to
the [forum], and bugs to the [issue tracker][issues].

![Logo][logo]

See [Error handling](#error-handling) and [FAQ: Why?](#faq-why).

## Error handling
## FAQ: Why?

[contrib]: CONTRIBUTING.md
[forum]: https://forum.example.com "Community forum"
[issues]: https://github.com/example/project/issues
[logo]: docs/logo.svg
takeaways: [text][label] plus [label]: url keeps URLs out of the prose
Labels are case-insensitive; [text] alone uses the text as label
Heading anchor rules differ per renderer; use explicit anchors when stability matters
pitfalls: Linking to #FAQ-Why? on GitHub; the generated anchor is lower case without punctuation: #faq-why.

quiz.q: What does [Docs] render as if there is no [docs]: definition anywhere?
quiz.explain: Without a matching definition the brackets aren't a link, so they render as plain text.

concepts.name: HTML inside Markdown
concepts.summary: Mix raw HTML into Markdown for what it can't express (details/summary, image sizes, anchors), and understand blank-line rules and sanitization.
concepts.why: A little HTML fills Markdown's gaps, but renderers strip or restrict it in ways you need to know.
concepts.body:
CommonMark passes **raw HTML** through to the output. Inline tags (`Ctrl`, ``, ``) work inside paragraphs. Block-level HTML such as `
`, `
` or `` starts an **HTML block** that continues until a blank line. The blank-line rule matters: Markdown is **not** processed inside an HTML block, but it is processed again after a blank line. So to use Markdown inside a `
` element, leave blank lines around the content: ```html
Show the logs - this list **is** rendered as Markdown
``` Useful HTML in docs: `
`/`` for collapsible sections, `` for sizing, `` for keys, `` for stable anchors, `
` inside table cells, and `` that don't appear in the output. Renderers **sanitize** HTML for security. GitHub strips `
concepts.code:
Press Ctrl+C to copy. H2O.
Full configuration example ```yaml server: port: 8080 ```
takeaways: Raw HTML passes through; an HTML block ends at a blank line
Leave blank lines inside <details> to get Markdown rendered there
Renderers sanitize HTML; sanitize user-supplied Markdown output yourself
pitfalls: Writing Markdown directly after <details> without a blank line and seeing it shown as raw text.

quiz.q: Why does a **bold** line right after <div> (no blank line) appear with literal asterisks?
options: It is still part of the HTML block, where Markdown isn't processed
Asterisks must be escaped in HTML
quiz.explain: An HTML block continues until a blank line, and its content is passed through as raw HTML.

concepts.name: Flavours, front matter and tooling
concepts.summary: Know CommonMark, GFM and other flavours, YAML front matter, diagrams and math blocks, MDX, and the linters and formatters that keep Markdown consistent.
concepts.why: The same file renders differently across GitHub, docs sites and editors, and tooling catches the differences.
concepts.body:
Original Markdown (2004) was loosely specified, and implementations disagreed. **CommonMark** is the precise specification most modern parsers follow; **GFM** is CommonMark plus tables, task lists, strikethrough, extended autolinks and HTML tag filtering. Other dialects add their own features: Pandoc Markdown (citations, definition lists), MultiMarkdown, Obsidian (wiki links `[[note]]`), MkDocs/Python-Markdown (admonitions `!!! note`, which aren't CommonMark-compliant in all details).

Common add-ons in docs systems:

- **Front matter**: a YAML block between `---` lines at the very top of the file, holding metadata (title, date, tags) for Jekyll, Hugo, Docusaurus, Astro and others. GitHub shows it as a table; a plain CommonMark parser would render it as a rule and a heading.
- **Diagrams**: fenced blocks with `mermaid` render as diagrams on GitHub, GitLab and many doc sites.
- **Math**: `$...$` and `$$...$$` (GitHub, GitLab, many sites) rendered with MathJax or KaTeX.
- **MDX**: Markdown that can also contain interactive page components (written in JSX, React's HTML-like syntax), used by Docusaurus and Next.js; stricter than Markdown (for example, `<` and `{` must be escaped).

Tooling:

- **markdownlint** (`markdownlint-cli2`) enforces consistent style: heading levels, list markers, blank lines around blocks, line length.
- **Prettier** formats Markdown: normalises lists, emphasis markers and table alignment.
- Link checkers (`lychee`, `markdown-link-check`) catch broken links in automated checks (CI).
concepts.code:
---
title: Deploying the API
tags: [ops, kubernetes]
---

# Deploying the API

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  dev[Push to main] --> ci[CI tests] --> deploy[Deploy to staging]
```

The cost is $O(n \log n)$ in the worst case.

<!-- .markdownlint.jsonc
{ "MD013": { "line_length": 100 }, "MD004": { "style": "dash" } }
$ npx markdownlint-cli2 "**/*.md"
$ npx prettier --write "**/*.md"
-->
takeaways: CommonMark is the spec; GFM adds tables, task lists and strikethrough
Front matter, mermaid diagrams and $math$ are widespread add-ons
markdownlint, Prettier and link checkers keep docs consistent in CI
pitfalls: Using a docs-site-only syntax (admonitions, wiki links) in a README that GitHub renders as plain text.

quiz.q: Where must YAML front matter appear for static site generators to read it?
options: At the end of the file
At the very top, between two --- lines
quiz.explain: Front matter is recognised only as the first thing in the file, delimited by --- lines.

concepts.name: How CommonMark parses: blocks, then inlines
concepts.summary: Understand CommonMark's two-phase parse: block structure (containers, leaf blocks, lazy continuation) first, then inline parsing of each paragraph and heading.
concepts.why: This model explains why indentation, blank lines and markers interact the way they do.
concepts.body:
CommonMark parses a document in **two phases**.

**Phase 1: block structure.** Lines are consumed one at a time to build a tree of blocks:

- **Container blocks** can hold other blocks: block quotes, list items, and lists (sequences of items).
- **Leaf blocks** hold text: paragraphs, headings, code blocks, HTML blocks, thematic breaks, link reference definitions.

For each new line the parser checks which open containers it continues (a `>` for a quote, enough indentation for a list item), then whether it starts a new block, and otherwise adds it as text to the open leaf. **Lazy continuation**: a line that would continue a paragraph can do so even without the container's markers, which is why the `>` can be omitted on continuation lines of a quoted paragraph.

Block structure always takes **precedence** over inline structure: whether a line is a list item, a code block or a heading is decided before any `*` or backtick on it is looked at.

**Phase 2: inlines.** The raw text of each paragraph and heading is parsed for code spans, emphasis, links, images, autolinks, raw HTML, escapes and line breaks. Link reference definitions collected in phase 1 are available here, which is why definitions can appear after their uses.

Code spans and autolinks bind more tightly than emphasis and links, so `` `*` `` is code, not emphasis.

Block parsing collects all definitions before inline parsing resolves links

concepts.name: List edge cases: indentation, tight and loose
concepts.summary: Master CommonMark's list rules: content indentation, the four-space pitfall, tight versus loose lists, starting numbers and when a list interrupts a paragraph.
concepts.why: List rendering is the most common source of 'it looks different on GitHub' bugs.
concepts.body:
The core rule: a list item's **content column** is set by the marker plus the spaces after it. For `- foo` it is column 2; for `10. foo` column 4. Anything that belongs to the item, such as a second paragraph, a code block or a sub-list, must be indented to at least that column. Consequences: - A sub-list under `1. item` needs **three** spaces, not two; under `- item`, two suffice. Using four everywhere usually works, but more than the content column plus three makes the line an indented code block. - After a list marker you can use 1 to 4 spaces. With 5 or more, the item starts with an indented code block. - Changing the bullet character (`-` to `*`) or the ordered delimiter (`.` to `)`) starts a **new list**. **Tight vs loose**: if any items are separated by blank lines, or an item contains blocks separated by blank lines, the list is **loose** and every item's text is wrapped in `

`, giving more spacing. One stray blank line changes the spacing of the whole list. **Starting number**: only the first item's number matters, up to 9 digits. To interrupt a paragraph, an ordered list must start with `1`, so a sentence that wraps onto a line beginning `14. ` doesn't become a list. A bullet list can interrupt a paragraph, but an empty list item cannot.

takeaways: Item content starts at marker width plus following spaces; nested blocks indent to that column
Blank lines between items or blocks make the whole list loose
Only a list starting at 1 can interrupt a paragraph
pitfalls: Indenting a sub-list under a numbered item with two spaces, which some renderers treat as a sibling item.

quiz.explain: The content of '1. ' starts at column 3, so nested blocks must be indented at least three spaces.

concepts.name: Emphasis rules: delimiter runs and flanking
concepts.summary: How CommonMark decides whether * and _ open or close emphasis: flanking delimiter runs, the intraword underscore rule and the rule of 3.
concepts.why: These rules explain every surprising asterisk and underscore, and why some inputs differ between parsers.
concepts.body: CommonMark's emphasis rules look complicated because they make ordinary text behave sensibly. The key idea is the **delimiter run**: a sequence of `*` or `_` characters. - A run is **left-flanking** (can open) if it's not followed by whitespace, and either not followed by punctuation or preceded by whitespace or punctuation. **Right-flanking** (can close) is the mirror image. - So `* not emphasis *` stays literal: the runs are surrounded by spaces. `2 * 3 * 4` is safe for the same reason. - `*` can open and close **inside words**: `un*believ*able`. `_` cannot open or close intraword, so `snake_case_word` is never emphasised. That's why underscores are safe in names used in code and `*` is preferred for intraword emphasis. Matching uses a delimiter stack: closers look back for the nearest compatible opener. `***a***` becomes `a`. The **rule of 3**: when one of the runs can both open and close, a pair whose combined length is a multiple of 3 doesn't match unless both lengths are multiples of 3, which keeps `*foo**bar**baz*` parsing as intended. Emphasis can't cross block boundaries, and code spans, links and autolinks take precedence: `*[link*](url)` doesn't put the link inside emphasis. Older parsers (original Markdown.pl, some non-CommonMark libraries) differ exactly in these corners, so test tricky input with the renderer that matters.
concepts.code: *emphasis* _emphasis_ **strong** __strong__ un*believ*able -> unbelievable un_believ_able -> un_believ_able (no intraword _ emphasis) snake_case_name -> unchanged 2 * 3 * 4 -> unchanged (spaces around the delimiters) * not emphasis * -> a list item! (block structure first) ***both*** -> both *foo**bar**baz* -> foobarbaz **unclosed -> literal **unclosed
takeaways: Delimiter runs must be left-flanking to open and right-flanking to close
_ never emphasises inside words; * does
Code spans and links take precedence over emphasis
pitfalls: Using _ for emphasis inside a word, as in re_use_able, and seeing literal underscores.

quiz.explain: Underscores flanked by alphanumerics on both sides can't open or close emphasis.
